analyses.title: Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations
analyses.research_question: Can long-form language-model generations be trained to communicate uncertainty such that downstream users form calibrated probabilistic forecasts, including under substantial domain and task shifts?
analyses.methodology: The paper defines linguistic calibration in terms of the calibration of probabilistic forecasts made by a downstream reader after consuming a long-form generation. It constructs synthetic supervision from question-answering datasets, first applies summary distillation to teach confidence-bearing long-form responses, and then performs decision-based reinforcement learning with a strictly proper scoring-rule objective using a surrogate reader. The authors calibrate Llama 2 7B and evaluate with simulated and human readers on in-distribution TriviaQA, out-of-distribution Jeopardy, SciQ, and BioASQ, plus a held-out person-biography generation task. Evaluation emphasizes reader expected calibration error and accuracy, with claim-level factuality evaluation for biographies.

key_findings.finding: Decision-based linguistic-calibration training substantially improves reader calibration relative to factuality-focused Llama 2 baselines while preserving comparable or better answer accuracy.
The reinforcement-learning variant maintains improved calibration under distribution shifts to Jeopardy, scientific QA, and biomedical QA rather than only on the training-domain task.
Calibration transfers zero-shot to a held-out biography-generation task, where claim-level evaluation shows improved calibration relative to non-confidence Llama-based methods.
A scalable simulated-reader evaluation tracks the intended downstream forecasting behavior sufficiently well to be validated against crowdworker evaluation.

The paper provides a decision-theoretic argument that appropriately calibrated downstream forecasts support informed decision making and connects weaker calibration notions to weaker decision guarantees.
The evaluation does not measure whether the source evidence behind each generated claim is complete, nor whether important supported information was omitted from the generation.
The reported distribution-shift evaluations are domain and task shifts rather than temporal-change evaluations with versioned or time-valid evidence.

limitations: Many generated uncertainty statements are relatively unambiguous numerical expressions, so the results do not establish calibration for more ambiguous natural-language uncertainty expressions across heterogeneous user populations.
Off-the-shelf QA datasets are used as proxies for questions encountered in real-world decision-making, which may limit ecological validity.
The training framework assumes white-box model access and fine-tuning, so it cannot directly calibrate completion-only API models.
The work evaluates calibration and factual accuracy rather than evidence completeness or systematic omission of relevant facts.
Its out-of-distribution experiments do not test temporally changing facts, evidence supersession, or citation validity over time.
raw_claims: Linguistic calibration is defined through the calibration of forecasts made by a reader after seeing a long-form model response.
The training procedure first teaches the model to express confidence and then optimizes downstream forecast calibration with reinforcement learning.
The reinforcement-learning model improves expected calibration error while retaining accuracy competitive with factuality-trained baselines.
The method is evaluated with both automated surrogate readers and human crowdworkers.
Calibration improvements transfer from TriviaQA to out-of-domain Jeopardy, SciQ, and BioASQ evaluations.
The calibrated model also transfers to person-biography generation without training on that generation task.
The released codebase contains prompts, checkpoints, method implementations, and dataset-related implementations.
The paper identifies representative real-world decision data and completion-only API models as important unresolved settings.

analyses.title: Claim-Level Confidence Calibration for Reliable Decision Making with Large Language Models
analyses.research_question: Can inference-time claim-level confidence estimation provide better calibrated and more decision-actionable uncertainty than assigning a single confidence value to an entire free-form LLM response?
analyses.methodology: The approach decomposes a response into atomic claims and computes confidence for each claim from self-verification or model probability signals, optionally combined with cross-sample consistency through a tuned convex mixture. Claims can then be retained or flagged using a confidence threshold, and calibration is evaluated using ECE, smECE, Brier score, AUROC, and selective-risk metrics. Experiments cover TriviaQA and TruthfulQA, seven baseline approaches, and six contemporary open- and closed-box models including reasoning models. Additional analyses examine calibration-mixture sensitivity, claim extraction, reliability diagrams, computational cost, and failure behavior on adversarial inputs.

key_findings.finding: Decomposing free-form responses into atomic claims and calibrating confidence at that level produces actionable per-claim uncertainty and reduces expected calibration error in factual-question settings.

Claim-level calibration can match or outperform response-level uncertainty baselines on mixed-correctness factual responses, although the magnitude and best method vary substantially by model and dataset.

False-premise and other adversarial inputs remain a major failure mode because models can assign high confidence to incorrect claims; the authors therefore recommend active verification or retrieval rather than confidence alone.

Reasoning-focused models show stronger verbalized uncertainty behavior, but extracting claims from their entire chain of thought can dilute useful final-answer confidence and final-answer-only extraction performs better.

The proposed inference pipeline is materially more expensive than one-call prompting, with the paper estimating roughly six times the API-call cost per query for its full claim extraction and verification workflow.
The experiments do not establish that calibrated claim confidence remains reliable under temporal knowledge change, source version changes, or sustained distribution drift.

Although thresholding permits claims to be retained or flagged, the paper does not directly evaluate whether threshold-based omission causes loss of important evidence or incomplete multi-source answers.

limitations: Confidence-only signals fail on adversarial false-premise inputs, requiring active verification, cross-examination, or retrieval.
Claim extraction from long reasoning traces can degrade calibration unless extraction is restricted to the final-answer span.
The complete method incurs multiple extraction and verification calls and is substantially more expensive than single-call baselines.
The evaluation is concentrated on TriviaQA and TruthfulQA rather than temporally evolving or explicitly distribution-shifted benchmarks.
Interdependent claims and hierarchical confidence are left as open research directions.
The paper does not directly measure evidence completeness or the utility loss caused by selectively suppressing claims.
raw_claims: A single response-level confidence score is too coarse when one answer contains both correct and incorrect claims.
The proposed pipeline decomposes responses into atomic claims and assigns confidence to each claim.
Confidence can combine a per-claim verification signal with consistency across independently sampled responses.
The approach is designed to work in closed-box settings through verbalized confidence as well as in open-box settings using probability information.
Experiments compare the method with sequence-likelihood, verbalized-confidence, parametric-calibration, HalluMeasure, and LMvsLM baselines.
Adversarial false-premise questions expose cases where confidence remains high despite incorrect claims.
Active verification is recommended when adversarial or misleading inputs are plausible.
The full proposed pipeline requires substantially more inference calls than ordinary few-shot or chain-of-thought prompting.

analyses.title: Only Say What You Know: Calibration-Aware Generation for Long-Form Factuality
analyses.research_question: Can a long-form reasoning model improve factuality without resorting to coarse whole-answer abstention by estimating the reliability of intermediate reasoning and selectively committing only to sufficiently reliable content?
analyses.methodology: The paper proposes Calibration-Aware Generation, which decouples reasoning exploration from final-answer commitment by attaching reliability levels to intermediate reasoning steps. Reliability supervision is derived by decomposing reasoning steps into atomic claims and scoring them with VeriScore using retrieved external evidence; Calibration-Aware Structured Supervision trains models to reason and reconstruct answers using those signals, while Calibration-Aware Policy Distillation transfers the behavior to smaller models. Experiments span five LLMs and five long-form factuality benchmarks, with additional testing on PopQA, GPQA, Vicuna QA, and RAG settings. Evaluation includes VeriScore-based factuality and helpfulness, ablations, reliability-versus-correctness AUC, threshold sensitivity, decoding time, and token usage.

key_findings.finding: Calibration-Aware Generation improves long-form factuality across multiple models and benchmarks, with the paper reporting gains of up to 13 percent without a substantial loss of overall informativeness in the evaluated settings.
Both calibrated exploration and selective commitment are necessary: removing either component consistently degrades performance across tested benchmarks and model sizes.

Selective commitment creates an explicit factuality-versus-coverage trade-off: lower reliability thresholds retain more information but admit more hallucinations, while higher thresholds improve factuality by discarding more potentially useful content.
Reliability estimates become better aligned with factual correctness than those of the corresponding vanilla models, as measured by AUC on Biography and FAVA.
Benefits extend beyond the main long-form benchmarks to knowledge-intensive QA, chatbot evaluation, and retrieval-augmented generation.
Suppressing unreliable answer content can reduce generation cost as well as hallucination; reported decoding-time reductions reach 37.36 percent for the evaluated Qwen models.
The work does not evaluate whether reliability-based omission preserves complete coverage of all decision-relevant facts or all available multi-source evidence.
The benchmarks do not test temporally superseded evidence, version-aware provenance, or calibration degradation as facts change over time.

limitations: Prioritizing highly reliable content can bias generation toward conservative and shorter answers, creating a factuality-informativeness trade-off.
Smaller models benefit more from policy distillation, indicating that accurate reliability estimation remains capacity-sensitive.
The factuality-supervision and evaluation pipeline depends on claim extraction, external retrieval, VeriScore, and GPT-5-backed evaluation components.
At the version reviewed, the authors state that code and data are not yet openly released and are intended for release upon acceptance.
The evaluation does not directly quantify omitted-but-supported information, evidence recall, or completeness of multi-source synthesis.
No dedicated temporal-change or longitudinal distribution-drift benchmark is evaluated.
raw_claims: Coarse answer-level abstention can reduce errors but also discards useful information that might have been retained safely.
Calibration-Aware Generation separates broad reasoning exploration from what the model ultimately commits to in its answer.
Intermediate reasoning steps receive reliability estimates derived from factual verification of their atomic claims.
Selective commitment uses those reliability signals to prioritize reliable reasoning when constructing the final response.
Experiments cover five model variants and five long-form factuality benchmarks.
Removing calibrated exploration or selective commitment harms performance.
Increasing the reliability threshold improves factuality but can remove useful information.
Calibration-aware models show stronger association between predicted reliability and factual correctness.
The method also improves results in knowledge-intensive QA, chatbot, and retrieval-augmented settings.
The reviewed version states that code and data will be released later rather than being currently available.

analyses.title: Program-Verifiable Evaluation for Temporal QA: Metrics for Evidence Validity
analyses.research_question: How can temporal question-answering systems be evaluated so that answer correctness is separated from whether the cited evidence was actually valid at the query time?
analyses.methodology: The paper defines a program-verifiable temporal-QA framework in which each question has a query time and each evidence document has an explicit validity interval. It introduces an oracle-answer diagnostic that fixes answers to gold while evaluating evidence selection, together with Recency-Aware Score, Recency-Aware Recall, Temporal Mismatch Rate, and evidence-attribution metrics. Evaluation uses the synthetic TimeFact-CEO benchmark and the semi-structured Wikidata-CEO corpus, comparing BM25, date and recency heuristics, and a lightweight lexico-temporal reranker. The paper additionally reports end-to-end evaluation, cross-corpus robustness, parameter sensitivity, and error analysis.

key_findings.finding: Answer correctness does not guarantee valid evidence: under oracle answers on TimeFact-CEO, 11.8 percent of selected citations are temporally invalid, with TMR 0.118 and RAS 0.903.
The proposed lexico-temporal reranker raises temporal-validity recall on TimeFact-CEO from 48.2 percent for BM25 to 88.2 percent, a 40.0 percentage-point improvement under oracle-answer evaluation.

On the noisy Wikidata-CEO corpus, the temporal reranker achieves RAS 0.936, RAR 0.934, and TMR 0.066, indicating that interval-aware evaluation remains useful outside the perfectly controlled synthetic benchmark.

First-stage retrieval coverage is the dominant bottleneck: coverage is 76.3 percent at K=3 and the authors attribute 82.4 percent of analyzed errors to gold evidence being absent from the retrieved candidate set.
Separating an oracle-answer diagnostic from end-to-end QA exposes evidence-timeliness failures that aggregate answer accuracy can hide.
The framework does not evaluate completeness of multi-document evidence because its primary protocol intentionally enforces a single top-1 evidence citation.

The evaluation covers changing temporal validity but does not establish generalization to unrestricted free-form multi-source generation, because experiments are confined to CEO-tenure facts with explicit intervals.

limitations: The framework assumes that evidence units have explicit validity intervals; purely implicit temporal signals require additional temporal grounding.
The minimum-citation policy evaluates one selected evidence document and therefore does not address multi-evidence synthesis or multi-hop temporal reasoning.
The main baselines are interpretable lexical, date, and recency heuristics rather than stronger neural or LLM-based temporal rerankers.
Both benchmarks use CEO-tenure facts, so cross-domain generalization remains unvalidated.
The framework evaluates evidence timeliness and attribution but not whether all decision-relevant evidence has been retrieved or summarized.
Its deterministic interval setting is substantially simpler than versioned free-form sources whose validity periods are uncertain or implicit.
raw_claims: A factually correct answer can still be supported by evidence that was invalid at the time referenced by the question.
The oracle-answer diagnostic fixes answer accuracy so evidence-timeliness errors can be measured independently.
RAS, RAR, and TMR quantify complementary aspects of temporal evidence validity.
TimeFact-CEO provides controlled synthetic validity intervals, whereas Wikidata-CEO contains noisier real-world interval data.
The lexico-temporal reranker substantially improves temporal evidence selection over lexical BM25 retrieval.
Retrieval coverage at K=3 is a major source of downstream evidence-selection error.
The framework uses exactly one cited evidence document in its minimum-citation evaluation protocol.
The experiments are restricted to CEO-tenure information with explicit validity intervals.
The paper references a public TimeFact-CEO code repository.

analyses.title: Minimal Evidence Group Identification for Claim Verification
analyses.research_question: Can claim-verification systems identify the smallest non-redundant set of evidence passages that is collectively sufficient to support a claim instead of retrieving a redundant union of all relevant evidence?
analyses.methodology: The paper formalizes a minimal evidence group as a sufficient evidence group for which no member is redundant. It converts WiCE and SciFact claim-verification data into WiCE-MEG and SciFact-MEG under explicit assumptions about full support, partial support, and non-labeled evidence. Its algorithm predicts whether candidate evidence groups fully, partially, or do not support the claim, then performs bottom-up merging of partially supporting groups while pruning redundant combinations; experiments use PaLM-2L for support prediction and redundancy checking. Intrinsic evaluation reports exact-match precision and best-soft-match precision, recall, and F0.5, while extrinsic evaluation tests evidence-budget effects in retrieval-augmented claim generation.

key_findings.finding: The proposed bottom-up MEG method substantially improves precision and F0.5 over direct LLM prediction and classic evidence-selection baselines on both WiCE-MEG and SciFact-MEG.
On WiCE-MEG, the proposed method reaches 0.809 soft-match precision and 0.684 F0.5, compared with 0.176 precision and 0.203 F0.5 for direct LLM prediction.
On SciFact-MEG, the proposed method reaches 0.612 soft-match precision and 0.533 F0.5, outperforming the reported direct and classic baselines on those precision-oriented measures.

The precision gains come with lower recall than several baselines, illustrating that selecting minimal sufficient evidence and exhaustively recovering all annotated evidence groups are different objectives.

Minimal evidence groups dramatically reduce evidence volume in the downstream claim-generation experiment while preserving performance close to much larger evidence sets under comparable computation budgets.
The available human annotations are not exhaustive enough to establish a true gold standard for all minimal sufficient evidence groups, which limits direct evaluation of evidence completeness.
Contradictory evidence is excluded from the task, so the framework does not establish completeness when supporting and conflicting sources coexist.
The experiments do not address temporal validity, evidence supersession, source versions, or performance under temporal distribution shift.

limitations: The task only models supporting versus non-supporting evidence and explicitly leaves contradiction handling for future work.
No purpose-built gold-standard MEG dataset exists, and the converted datasets require assumptions that annotated evidence groups are sufficient and minimal.
Human annotators generally do not enumerate every possible valid evidence group, so measured recall cannot represent exhaustive evidence completeness.
The approach requires combinatorial evidence-set reasoning and uses pruning because explicit combination checking is NP-hard.
Experiments rely on PaLM-2L prompting, so behavior may depend on the underlying support classifier and redundancy checker.
The work does not model temporal validity, changing evidence versions, or distribution drift.
raw_claims: A minimal evidence group must collectively support the claim while containing no redundant evidence passage.
The method searches from smaller evidence combinations upward and stops after finding fully supporting groups at the smallest discovered size.
Candidate combinations predicted as already fully supporting or non-supporting are not expanded further.
WiCE-MEG and SciFact-MEG are derived from existing claim-verification datasets rather than newly exhaustively annotated MEG corpora.
The proposed approach obtains higher precision-oriented MEG scores than direct LLM prompting and classic baselines.
Its MEG predictions have lower recall than some competing approaches despite their higher precision.
Using minimal evidence can reduce the number of evidence sentences supplied to downstream generation.
Contradictory evidence is outside the evaluated task.
Human evidence annotations are not guaranteed to contain every valid minimal evidence group.
